title: 语言模型隐私泄露的技术演进
content_md: # 语言模型隐私泄露的技术演进：机制、比较与边界 ## 摘要 本文综述了语言模型隐私泄露与防护的演进历程。研究起源于语言模型精确记忆训练数据带来的信息重构风险，其评价对象现已从生成精确文本扩展至非生成任务及文本嵌入。威胁模型日趋复杂，涵盖黑盒提取、更新快照分析、联邦服务器参数篡改及数据投毒等新型攻击，驱动评估指标向低假阳率及似然比检验修正。在防御端，研究从早期数据干预与全局加噪向正向传播干预、选择性加噪、参数高效微调及解码后处理等多维组合发展。然而，自然语言特征的高度语境化与传统差分隐私的结构化独立假设存在深刻矛盾；大规模语言模型在超高维度下的高准确率需求与严格的隐私安全保障仍面临内在理论不兼容和效用严重退化的双重挑战。 ## 研究问题与技术前史 语言模型隐私泄露的研究起源于神经网络对训练数据的记忆特性及其带来的信息重构风险。在早期探索中，研究者试图厘清语言模型记忆行为与数据泄露之间的映射关系。针对LSTM等循环神经网络语言模型的分析表明，困惑度（perplexity）较低的句子更易被模型深度记忆，从而成为隐私攻击的脆弱点。为了在源头阻断这一风险，早期的防御分支之一是直接对训练材料进行干预，通过语义变异（mutating）训练数据来实现模型的“去记忆化”（dememorization），且该机制在评估中能够在不折损模型效用的前提下缓解数据泄露[11]。随着隐私保护理论的引入，差分隐私（DP）成为演进路线上的另一核心分支。在循环语言模型的早期联邦训练中，研究者通过改造联邦平均算法，实现了用户级别的差分隐私保障；该机制的核心发现是，当参与用户规模足够大时，引入隐私噪声的主要代价是计算开销的增加，而非传统认为的模型效用骤降[1]。当研究主体向BERT等预训练语言模型演进时，隐私注入的机制发生了分化。与传统的全局梯度加噪不同，部分研究转向局部差分隐私（Local DP）设定，通过在输入文本或词嵌入（token embeddings）等不同前向阶段施加约束，探索隐私自适应的预训练方法，从而缓解了自然语言理解任务在直接应用隐私约束时的适配问题[21]。与此同时，分布式架构的演进催生了对联邦学习场景下语言模型隐私威胁的重新审视。尽管联邦学习通过仅传输模型更新而非原始数据来构建初步防御，但早期的威胁模型测量表明，这种架构并未彻底消除隐私泄露风险。无论是恶意聚合服务器还是普通参与节点，均可通过深度梯度泄露（Deep Gradients Leakage）攻击或生成对抗网络攻击，从共享参数中逆向推断出用户级别的训练样本。这一阶段的研究不仅明确了推理攻击推断样本与投毒攻击破坏模型完整性的机制差别，也促使后续防护策略从单一的数据端掩码向聚合端的安全汇聚技术演进[49]。 ## 评价对象、威胁模型与测量 语言模型的隐私泄露研究在评价对象、威胁模型与测量方法上经历了系统性演进。 **评价对象的延伸** 早期的评价对象集中于生成式语言模型对训练数据的精确记忆，研究表明模型参数规模越大，记忆现象越严重且脆弱性越高[4]。随着研究深入，评估对象扩展至非生成式任务。文本分类模型同样存在数据提取风险，攻击者可利用目标标签的似然度推断输入中缺失的词元[43]；或通过模型反演，利用预训练生成模型（如GPT-2）构建模板并依据分类器反馈进行扰动，从而重建私有训练文本[52]。此外，文本嵌入（Embeddings）也成为重要的评价对象。研究证实，密集嵌入向量不仅保留了语义，还可通过逆向优化恢复大部分输入词汇，甚至被用于推断疾病部位或作者身份等独立于主任务的敏感属性[5][7]。 **威胁模型的复杂化** 威胁模型从简单的黑盒查询演进为多阶段、动态与对抗性环境下的复杂攻击。在模型提取攻击中，攻击者仅需向API发送随机词序列（乱码数据），即可成功克隆BERT类模型[3]；这种攻击甚至能从单语受害者模型中提取出具备多语言能力的副本[9]。更为严重的是，这种提取过程会继承并暴露原始数据的隐私，使得针对克隆副本的属性推断攻击同样能够窃取受害者训练集信息[38]。 在动态更新场景下，攻击者利用模型更新前后的参数快照实施差分分析，可通过束搜索算法精准提取新增的对话数据[2]；对于智能回复等微调应用，灰盒快照攻击通过对比微调前后的标记概率变化，能够成功提取密码和邮箱等敏感模式[25]。在联邦学习等去中心化架构中，威胁模型被进一步强化：恶意服务器可通过部署篡改的参数字典，单独提取Transformer的标记嵌入与位置嵌入，进而高保真地重建长序列用户文本[28]。此外，数据投毒成为一种新型机制，攻击者仅需篡改不足0.1%的训练数据，便能引导模型将特定目标视为异常，从而使成员推理等隐私推断的成功率跃升一至两个数量级[56]。 **测量机制的校准** 随着攻击机制的精细化，隐私泄露的测量指标也得到了根本性校正。过往研究常采用平均分类准确率来衡量成员推理攻击，但这一对称指标掩盖了真实的安全威胁。现代测量主张在极低假阳性率（如<0.1%）下计算真阳性率，以评估攻击是否能以高置信度识别特定成员[16]。在针对掩码语言模型（MLM）的评估中，传统的单一模型置信度测量往往失效；通过引入参考模型构建基于能量的似然比假设检验，攻击在1%假阳性率下的效力可提升数十倍，AUC指标也获得了显著修正[45]。为了统一复杂场景的测量基准，研究者提出了参数化评估框架（如KART），将隐私泄露风险分解为先验知识、数据匿名化程度、外部语料资源及目标实体等维度，为语言模型隐私审计提供了系统性标准[13]。 ## 基准构建、检测与防护 语言模型隐私防护已演进为在训练、微调及推理阶段组合数据去重、选择性差分隐私与生成扰动的多维机制。早期全局差分隐私（DP）虽提供理论保证，但导致显著的效用下降。为优化隐私与效用的联合空间，[20]引入对抗鉴别器与三元组损失正则化；[44]结合编辑与随机化机制实现机密编辑训练（CRT），在特定任务上维持了与基线相近的困惑度。针对特定实体的隐私泄露，[23]提出选择性差分隐私（S-DP），仅对通过策略函数检测到的敏感词元添加噪声；[57]进一步结合用户与实体采样，提出用户-实体差分隐私（UeDP）以优化模型敏感度上界。在数据层面，[29]发现模型记忆率与训练集中序列重复次数呈超线性相关，数据去重可显著降低记忆攻击的成功率。[55]验证了T5模型的跨度破坏目标比传统的下个词预测更具抗记忆性。在微调与分布式架构下，大模型的参数规模放大了DP噪声。为降低计算与隐私成本，[36]在微调阶段引入Edgeworth会计师，提供非渐进的有限样本隐私边界。[14]通过避免实例化线性层的逐样本梯度，使得在适度语料上直接进行DP-SGD微调的内存开销与非隐私训练相当。在联邦学习场景中，[54]提出部分嵌入更新（PEU）以降低大词表传输中的DP噪声；[30]通过输入加密优化问题（LODA）直接学习模糊化数据特征以防御梯度泄露；[46]则证明在训练时冻结词嵌入可有效防御大批量文本的梯度反演恢复攻击（FILM）。针对免重训的后置防护，机制开始向推理端转移。[33]在解码阶段对输出概率分布应用轻量级扰动，通过后处理特性继承隐私优势。[51]的SubMix协议通过集成模型的子样本聚合松弛群组DP，在预测时限制单用户特有信息的泄露。[40]提出知识遗忘机制，通过对目标序列执行梯度上升，在先验已知易受攻击数据时提供比预处理更强的经验隐私保证。 ## 有效性、鲁棒性和外推边界 语言模型隐私攻防的演进不仅体现在技术手段的更迭，更在于其有效性、鲁棒性及外推边界的显著拓展。在攻击外推边界方面，早期的模型逆向和成员推理通常依赖严苛的先验假设。然而，近期的研究发现迁移学习打破了这一安全错觉：微调模型与预训练基座在权重分布上存在极高相似性，攻击者仅需利用框架或硬件的特定计算签名，即可推断出黑盒模型的基座架构并逆向完整权重[47]。与此同时，数据恢复攻击的鲁棒性也得到增强。传统重构依赖目标样本的真实标签预测，但基于分布判别的提取机制无需真实类别先验，仅通过伪标签预测与分布差异即可实现相似的隐私数据还原率，极大拓宽了预训练模型泄漏威胁的外推边界[48]。 在防御机制的有效性演进上，差分隐私（DP）的实施路径出现了从反向传播向正向传播和参数高效微调的分支转移。传统的DP-SGD在反向传播阶段对梯度进行裁剪与加噪，不仅引入梯度偏差，还会在大模型上引发严重的内存开销。相比之下，差分隐私正向传播机制通过在正向阶段直接对潜层表示进行裁剪加噪，并结合微批次子采样实现隐私放大，从而在保持梯度无偏的同时大幅缓解了性能降级[10]。此外，模型规模与隐私效用之间展现出反直觉的关联外推性：在参数高效微调框架下，随着语言模型参数量级的提升，其在注入相同隐私预算噪声时的鲁棒性反而更强，能够在维持严格隐私约束下逼近非隐私模型的效用表现[12]。 针对分布式与表示层的隐私保护，机制有效性从单一表示扰动向混合理论约束演进。在联邦学习场景中，早期的实例编码机制主要通过对预训练模型的输入表示应用单次密钥加密或混合以抵御梯度窃听[8]。然而，由于缺乏理论隐私下界，单纯的实例编码极易受重构攻击破解。为此，后继方法将差分隐私机制与实例编码深度融合，通过在特征提取层引入拉普拉斯或高斯噪声，建立了抵抗重构攻击的可证明隐私边界[34]。此外，在对话聊天机器人外推至用户级特征保护时，隐藏状态极易过度拟合发音者的私人画像。通过在防御目标中引入互信息损失与KL散度惩罚，可直接将攻击者对人物属性的后验预测分布扁平化，在阻断画像推断攻击的同时，有效保留了语言模型的生成鲁棒性[61]。 ## 实验证据与方法比较 语言模型隐私泄露的实验评估经历了从单一场景向标准化框架与细粒度指标的演进。早期研究因攻击假设不一难以横向比较，研究者提出KART（知识、匿名化、资源与目标）参数化框架以统一成员推理等泄露场景的定义标准[6]。在评价指标层面，除了传统的生成重叠率，研究者通过对比私有模型与公共模型生成的独有序列数量，量化了模型生成训练集中独有句子片段的泄露风险[19]；同时采用“暴露度”（Exposure）指标评估随机金丝雀样本提取对攻击者猜测熵的降低程度[41]。面对大型语言模型庞大的生成解空间，通过正则表达式将复杂的记忆验证规则转化为有限状态自动机查询，不仅规避了临时采样的偏差，还显著提升了评估的系统效率与统计覆盖率[58]。 在比较机制与对照条件方面，模型架构与规模表现出显著的隐私脆弱性差异。研究表明，由于注意力模块及偏置参数的设计特征，Transformer架构整体比传统卷积神经网络更容易受到多种隐私推理攻击[39]。在语言模型内部，掩码语言模型的经验隐私泄露水平通常低于自回归模型[15]。关于模型规模的实验结果呈现出多维度的冲突现象：一方面，小型模型的经验泄露总体低于大型模型[15]，且模型复杂度与预训练数据量的增加会正向推高信息泄露风险[60]；另一方面，动态跟踪训练过程发现，大模型不仅能以更少优化步数完成精确记忆（特别是优先记忆作为数据标识符的名词与数字），甚至在不过拟合的情况下保留更多早期训练记忆，导致其遗忘率反而低于小规模基线[42]。此外，实验证实模型虽然能够深度记忆邮箱地址等私有片段，但缺乏将上下文特征与特定实体强关联的能力，导致零样本条件下的直接提取成功率极低[26]。 针对分布式部署与多模态融合条件的评估揭示了不同环境下的真实威胁边界。在联邦学习框架中，中心化学习下普遍存在的非预期记忆倾向，会因联邦架构自带的按用户聚类机制及大批次聚合而得到大幅缓解[24]。然而，理论上的差分隐私界限在联邦环境中可能过于保守，基于恶意客户端构造特定金丝雀样本并观测异常模型更新的经验测量表明，实际的隐私暴露风险（经验$\epsilon$值）比理论上限低两至七倍[27]。在多模态融合场景中，即便攻击者只能通过合成音频进行端到端语音识别的黑盒查询，利用基线与金丝雀样本的词错率差异，依然能检测出融合语言模型对仅出现一次的文本序列的无意记忆，且该记忆水平随模型容量增加而放大[31]。 防护机制的引入进一步凸显了隐私与效用的权衡冲突。在多语言情感分析等任务中，差分隐私的强噪声注入会严重损害模型的下游效用[60]；但在层次化文本分类等特定任务中，针对长文本优化的Transformer模型即便在较大的差分隐私参数下，也能在完全防御白盒成员推理攻击的同时维持合理的预测性能[18]。相比于后置扰动，在预处理阶段执行严格的自动去标识化，不仅不会阻碍临床语言模型的领域适应，反而在部分下游任务中实现了效用的微幅提升，为规避记忆风险提供了低成本的对照验证方案[35]。 ## 局限、效率与开放问题 语言模型隐私保护的演进不仅受制于工程层面的技术瓶颈，更面临理论假设与自然语言特性的根本失配。传统数据清理与差分隐私（DP）机制高度依赖数据的结构化特征与逻辑独立性假设，这与自然语言高度语境化且缺乏明确个体或相邻界定的本质产生了直接冲突[32][59]。在基础模型层面，这种理论局限性被进一步放大：由于处理异构用户数据需要满足极高的所罗门诺夫-柯尔莫哥洛夫复杂度，模型必须通过深度记忆来实现任务泛化，这使得在超高维参数空间下追求高准确率与保障严格隐私安全，在数学基础上存在难以调和的内在不兼容性[50]。 当前主流的模型防护机制在特定边界条件下表现出明显的失效特征。在词级别差分隐私中，距离度量机制容易在长文本序列中隐性吸收隐私损失，导致在未能有效掩盖原作者风格特征的情况下过早消耗了理论隐私预算[53]。同时，针对文本表示层的实例编码混合机制同样缺乏严密的安全性下界，攻击者无需付出高昂的计算代价，即可通过模型逆向攻击以高成功率重建出原始敏感文本向量[22]。此外，即便防御方将嵌入层置于黑盒部署环境中以隐藏内部状态，成员推断攻击依然能绕过高成本的影子模型训练，将底层语义泄露风险直接穿透至下游的文本分类与自然语言生成任务中[17]。 在部署成本与训练效率维度，差分隐私的引入从根本上打破了语言模型的常规缩放定律。在非隐私环境下普遍适用的“模型参数越大性能越好”经验法则在DP-SGD优化中彻底失效，不同复杂度任务的隐私防护呈现出高度的架构与策略依赖：例如，受限于梯度裁剪与噪声注入，参数量更小的蒸馏模型虽能通过降低显存占用换取更大的训练批次，但在面对多类别序列标注等复杂任务时，其性能反而出现严重退化[62]。更为严峻的未解决问题在于隐私效用与算法公平性之间的冲突，差分隐私的梯度更新会对少数群体的特征表示产生不成比例的损害，在稳健深度学习体系中呈现出隐私预算与公平性指标的对数级负相关；理论推导证明，当模型被同时强制要求满足绝对差分隐私与严格组等风险公平时，其预测结果将完全退化为与输入数据无关的平凡输出[37]。 ## 结论 语言模型的隐私泄露不仅源于庞大参数规模的记忆特征，也植根于分布训练架构的固有脆弱性。攻防对抗实践表明，差分隐私与实例编码等防护手段虽能阶段性阻断敏感数据的提取，但随之升级的分布判别与逆向恢复技术不断突破安全边界。现有的防护策略难以充分适应长序列上下文依赖的语言特征，并在隐私预算、计算开销、模型效用与算法公平性之间面临严峻的权衡困境。未来的演进需要突破结构化数据隐私概念的局限，构建更契合自然语言生成机制的细粒度审计框架，并探索能在基础参数层面解耦语言泛化能力与个体数据记忆的内生性安全模型范式。 ## source_intervals.text: Learning Differentially Private Recurrent Language Models We demonstrate that it is possible to train large recurrent language models with user-level differential privacy guarantees with only a negligible cost in predictive accuracy. Our work builds on recent advances in the training of deep networks on user-partitioned data and privacy accounting for stochastic gradient descent. In particular, we add user-level privacy protection to the federated averaging algorithm, which makes "large step" updates from user-level data. Our work demonstrates that given a dataset with a sufficiently large number of users (a requirement easily met by even small internet-scale datasets), achieving differential privacy comes at the cost of increased computation, rather than in decreased utility as in most prior work. We find that our private LSTM language models are quantitatively and qualitatively similar to un-noised models when trained on a large dataset.

source_intervals.text: Analyzing Information Leakage of Updates to Natural Language Models To continuously improve quality and reflect changes in data, machine learning applications have to regularly retrain and update their core models. We show that a differential analysis of language model snapshots before and after an update can reveal a surprising amount of detailed information about changes in the training data. We propose two new metrics---\emph{differential score} and \emph{differential rank}---for analyzing the leakage due to updates of natural language models. We perform leakage analysis using these metrics across models trained on several different datasets using different methods and configurations. We discuss the privacy implications of our findings, propose mitigation strategies and evaluate their effect. Model Extraction of BERT-based APIs We study the problem of model extraction in natural language processing, in which an adversary with only query access to a victim model attempts to reconstruct a local copy of that model. Assuming that both the adversary and victim model fine-tune a large pretrained language model such as BERT (Devlin et al. 2019), we show that the adversary does not need any real training data to successfully mount the attack. In fact, the attacker need not even use grammatical or semantically meaningful queries: we show that random sequences of words coupled with task-specific heuristics form effective queries for model extraction on a diverse set of NLP tasks including natural language inference and question answering. Our work thus highlights an exploit only made feasible by the shift towards transfer learning methods within the NLP community: for a query budget of a few hundred dollars, an attacker can extract a model that performs only slightly worse than the victim model. Finally, we study two defense strategies against model extraction---membership classification and API watermarking---which while successful against naive adversaries, are ineffective against more sophisticated ones. source_intervals.text: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models It has become common to publish large (billion parameter) language models that have been trained on private datasets. This paper demonstrates that in such settings, an adversary can perform a training data extraction attack to recover individual training examples by querying the language model. We demonstrate our attack on GPT-2, a language model trained on scrapes of the public Internet, and are able to extract hundreds of verbatim text sequences from the model's training data. These extracted examples include (public) personally identifiable information (names, phone numbers, and email addresses), IRC conversations, code, and 128-bit UUIDs. Our attack is possible even though each of the above sequences are included in just one document in the training data. We comprehensively evaluate our extraction attack to understand the factors that contribute to its success. Worryingly, we find that larger models are more vulnerable than smaller models. We conclude by drawing lessons and discussing possible safeguards for training large language models. Introduction Language models (LMs)-statistical models which assign a probability to a sequence of words-are fundamental to many natural language processing tasks. Modern neural-networkbased LMs use very large model architectures (e.g., 175 billion parameters [7]) and train on massive dat

enerations of LMs are emerging and becoming building blocks for a range of real-world applications. Conclusion For large language models to be widely adopted, they must address the training data memorization problems that we have identified. Our

extraction attacks are practical and efficient, and can recover hundreds of training examples from a model, even when they are contained in just one training document. Our analysis is best viewed as a cautionary tale of what could happen when training large LMs on sensitive data. Even though our attacks target GPT-2 (which allows us to ensure that our work is not harmful), the same techniques apply to any LM. Moreover, because memorization gets worse as LMs become larger, we expect that these vulnerabilities will become significantly more important in the future. There will therefore need to be techniques developed to specifically address our attacks. Training with differentiallyprivate techniques is one method for mitigating privacy leakage, however, we believe that it will be necessary to develop new methods that can train models at this extreme scale (e.g., billions of parameters) without sacrificing model accuracy or training time. More generally, there are many open questions that we hope will be investigated further, including why models memorize, the dangers of memorization, and how to prevent memorization. source_intervals.text: Information Leakage in Embedding Models Embeddings are functions that map raw input data to low-dimensional vector representations, while preserving important semantic information about the inputs. Pre-training embeddings on a large amount of unlabeled data and fine-tuning them for downstream tasks is now a de facto standard in achieving state of the art learning in many domains. We demonstrate that embeddings, in addition to encoding generic semantics, often also present a vector that leaks sensitive information about the input data. We develop three classes of attacks to systematically study information that might be leaked by embeddings. First, embedding vectors can be inverted to partially recover some of the input data. As an example, we show that our attacks on popular sentence embeddings recover between 50\%--70\% of the input words (F1 scores of 0.5--0.7). Second, embeddings may reveal sensitive attributes inherent in inputs and independent of the underlying semantic task at hand. Attributes such as authorship of text can be easily extracted by training an inference model on just a handful of labeled embedding vectors. Third, embedding models leak moderate amount of membership information for infrequent training data inputs. source_intervals.text: KART: Parameterization of Privacy Leakage Scenarios from Pre-trained Language Models For the safe sharing pre-trained language models, no guidelines exist at present owing to the difficulty in estimating the upper bound of the risk of privacy leakage. One problem is that previous studies have assessed the risk for different real-world privacy leakage scenarios and attack methods, which reduces the portability of the findings. To tackle this problem, we represent complex real-world privacy leakage scenarios under a universal parameterization, \textit{Knowledge, Anonymization, Resource, and Target} (KART). KART parameterization has two merits: (i) it clarifies the definition of privacy leakage in each experiment and (ii) it improves the comparability of the findings of risk assessments. We show that previous studies can be simply reviewed by parameterizing the scenarios with KART. We also demonstrate privacy risk assessments in different scenarios under the same attack method, which suggests that KART helps approximate the upper bound of risk under a specific attack or scenario. We believe that KART helps integrate past and future findings on privacy risk and will contribute to a standard for sharing language models. source_intervals.text: Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models Recently, a new paradigm of building general-purpose language models (e.g., Google’s Bert and OpenAI’s GPT-2) in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for text feature extraction, a standard procedure in NLP systems that converts texts to vectors (i.e., embeddings) for downstream modeling, has arisen and starts to find its application in various downstream NLP tasks and real world systems (e.g., Google’s search engine [6]). To obtain general-purpose text embeddings, these language models have highly complicated architectures with millions of learnable parameters and are usually pretrained on billions of sentences before being utilized. As is widely recognized, such a practice indeed improves the state-of-the-art performance of many downstream NLP tasks. However, the improved utility is not for free. We find the text embeddings from general-purpose language models would capture much sensitive information from the plain text. Once being accessed by the adversary, the embeddings can be reverse-engineered to disclose sensitive information of the victims for further harassment. Although such a privacy risk can impose a real threat to the future leverage of these promising NLP tools, there are neither published attacks nor systematic evaluations by far for the mainstream industry-level language models. To bridge this gap, we present the fi

rst systematic study on the privacy risks of 8 state-of-the-art language models with 4 diverse case studies. By constructing 2 novel attack classes, our study demonstrates the aforementioned privacy risks do exist and can impose practical threats to the application of general-purpose language models on sensitive data covering identity, genome, healthcare and location. For

example, we show the adversary with nearly no prior knowledge can achieve about 75% accuracy when inferring the precise disease site from Bert embeddings of patients’ medical descriptions. As possible countermeasures, we propose 4 different defenses (via rounding, differential privacy, adversarial training and subspace projection) to obfuscate the unprotected embeddings for mitigation purpose. With extensive evaluations, we also provide a preliminary analysis on the utility-privacy trade-off brought by each defense, which we hope may foster future mitigation researches.

source_intervals.text: TextHide: Tackling Data Privacy in Language Understanding Tasks An unsolved challenge in distributed or federated learning is to effectively mitigate privacy risks without slowing down training or reducing accuracy. In this paper, we propose TextHide aiming at addressing this challenge for natural language understanding tasks. It requires all participants to add a simple encryption step to prevent an eavesdropping attacker from recovering private text data. Such an encryption step is efficient and only affects the task performance slightly. In addition, TextHide fits well with the popular framework of fine-tuning pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) for any sentence or sentence-pair task. We evaluate TextHide on the GLUE benchmark, and our experiments show that TextHide can effectively defend attacks on shared gradients or representations and the averaged accuracy reduction is only $1.9\%$. We also present an analysis of the security of TextHide using a conjecture about the computational intractability of a mathematical problem. source_intervals.text: The Thieves on Sesame Street Are Polyglots — Extracting Multilingual Models from Monolingual APIs Pre-training in natural language processing makes it easier for an adversary with only query access to a victim model to reconstruct a local copy of the victim by training with gibberish input data paired with the victim’s labels for that data. We discover that this extraction process extends to local copies initialized from a pre-trained, multilingual model while the victim remains monolingual. The extracted model learns the task from the monolingual victim, but it generalizes far better than the victim to several other languages. This is done without ever showing the multilingual, extracted model a well-formed input in any of the languages for the target task. We also demonstrate that a few real examples can greatly improve performance, and we analyze how these results shed light on how such extraction methods succeed. Introduction Deploying machine learning models typically involves significant cost, including the expense of data acquisition, data cleaning, and model training and tuning. Recent work by Krishna et al. (2020) has demonstrated that deployed NLP models can be stolen by adversaries by querying victim models with gibberish input data that consists of random sequences of words. In particular, they showed that the following approach is sufficient for stealing text class

Combining it with model stealing, or extracting, we demonstrate cross-lingual transfer of task-specific knowledge stolen from a monolingual victim model without collecting a single grammatically correct sentence in any language. Our investigation has ramifications for the discussion of model APIs as intellectual property and motivates the need to build defenses against such attacks. Since models could be deployed by adversaries in multiple languages without collecting real examples in any, defenses such as watermarking would be rendered useless. source_intervals.text: DeepMemory: Model-based Memorization Analysis of Deep Neural Language Models The neural network model is having a significant impact on many real-world applications. Unfortunately, the increasing popularity and complexity of these models also amplifies their security and privacy challenges, with privacy leakage from training data being one of the most prominent issues. In this context, prior studies proposed to analyze the abstraction behavior of neural network models, e.g., RNN, to understand their robustness. However, the existing research rarely addresses privacy breaches caused by memorization in neural language models. To fill this gap, we propose a novel approach, DeepMemory, that analyzes memorization behavior for a neural language model. We first construct a memorization-analysis-oriented model, taking both training data and a neural language model as input. We then build a semantic first-order Markov model to bind the constructed memorization-analysis-oriented model to the training data to analyze memorization distribution. Finally, we apply our approach to address data leakage issues associated with memorization and to assist in dememorization. We evaluate our approach on one of the most popular neural language models, the LSTM-based language model, with three public datasets, namely, WikiText-103, WMT2017, and IWSLT2016. We find that sentences in the studied datasets

with low perplexity are more likely to be memorized. Our approach achieves an average AUC of 0.73 in automatically identifying data leakage issues during assessment. We also show that with the assistance of DeepMemory, data breaches due to memorization of neural language models can be successfully mitigated by mutating training data without reducing the performance of neural language models.

source_intervals.text: Differentially Private Fine-tuning of Language Models We give simpler, sparser, and faster algorithms for differentially private fine-tuning of large-scale pre-trained language models, which achieve the state-of-the-art privacy versus utility tradeoffs on many standard NLP tasks. We propose a meta-framework for this problem, inspired by the recent success of highly parameter-efficient methods for fine-tuning. Our experiments show that differentially private adaptations of these approaches outperform previous private algorithms in three important dimensions: utility, privacy, and the computational and memory cost of private training. On many commonly studied datasets, the utility of private models approaches that of non-private models. For example, on the MNLI dataset we achieve an accuracy of $87.8\%$ using RoBERTa-Large and $83.5\%$ using RoBERTa-Base with a privacy budget of $\epsilon = 6.7$. In comparison, absent privacy constraints, RoBERTa-Large achieves an accuracy of $90.2\%$. Our findings are similar for natural language generation tasks. source_intervals.text: KART: Privacy Leakage Framework of Language Models Pre-trained with Clinical Records Nowadays, mainstream natural language processing (NLP) is empowered by pre-trained language models. In the biomedical domain, only models pre-trained with anonymized data have been published. source_intervals.text: On the privacy-utility trade-off in differentially private hierarchical text classification Hierarchical text classification consists in classifying text documents into a hierarchy of classes and sub-classes. Although artificial neural networks have proved useful to perform this task, unfortunately they can leak training data information to adversaries due to training data memorization. Using differential privacy during model training can mitigate leakage attacks against trained models, enabling the models to be shared safely at the cost of reduced model accuracy. This work investigates the privacy-utility trade-off in hierarchical text classification with differential privacy guarantees, and identifies neural network architectures that offer superior trade-offs. To this end, we use a white-box membership inference attack to empirically assess the information leakage of three widely used neural network architectures. We show that large differential privacy parameters already suffice to completely mitigate membership inference attacks, thus resulting only in a moderate decrease in model utility. More specifically, for large datasets with long texts we observed Transformer-based models to achieve an overall favorable privacy-utility trade-off, while for smaller datasets with shorter texts convolutional neural networks are preferable. source_intervals.text: Deduplicating Training Data Mitigates Privacy Risks in Language Models Past work has shown that large language models are susceptible to privacy attacks, where adversaries generate sequences from a trained model and detect which sequences are memorized from the training set. In this work, we show that the success of these attacks is largely due to duplication in commonly used web-scraped training sets. We first show that the rate at which language models regenerate training sequences is superlinearly related to a sequence's count in the training set. For instance, a sequence that is present 10 times in the training data is on average generated ~1000 times more often than a sequence that is present only once. We next show that existing methods for detecting memorized sequences have near-chance accuracy on non-duplicated training sequences. Finally, we find that after applying methods to deduplicate training data, language models are considerably more secure against these types of privacy attacks. Taken together, our results motivate an increased focus on deduplication in privacy-sensitive applications and a reevaluation of the practicality of existing privacy attacks. source_intervals.text: Defense Against Gradient Leakage Attacks via Learning to Obscure Data Federated learning is considered as an effective privacy-preserving learning mechanism that separates the client's data and model training process. However, federated learning is still under the risk of privacy leakage because of the existence of attackers who deliberately conduct gradient leakage attacks to reconstruct the client data. Recently, popular strategies such as gradient perturbation methods and input encryption methods have been proposed to defend against gradient leakage attacks. Nevertheless, these defenses can either greatly sacrifice the model performance, or be evaded by more advanced attacks. In this paper, we propose a new defense method to protect the privacy of clients' data by learning to obscure data. Our defense method can generate synthetic samples that are totally distinct from the original samples, but they can also maximally preserve their predictive features and guarantee the model performance. Furthermore, our defense strategy makes the gradient leakage attack and its variants extremely difficult to reconstruct the client data. Through extensive experiments, we show that our proposed defense method obtains better privacy protection while preserving high accuracy compared with state-of-the-art methods. source_intervals.text: How Does a Deep Learning Model Architecture Impact Its Privacy? As a booming research area in the past decade, deep learning technologies have been driven by big data collected and processed on an unprecedented scale. However, the sensitive information in the collected training data raises privacy concerns. Recent research indicated that deep learning models are vulnerable to various privacy attacks, including membership inference attacks, attribute inference attacks, and gradient inversion attacks. It is noteworthy that the performance of the attacks varies from model to model. In this paper, we conduct empirical analyses to answer a fundamental question: Does model architecture affect model privacy? We investigate several representative model architectures from CNNs to Transformers, and show that Transformers are generally more vulnerable to privacy attacks than CNNs. We further demonstrate that the micro design of activation layers, stem layers, and bias parameters, are the major reasons why CNNs are more resilient to privacy attacks than Transformers. We also find that the presence of attention modules is another reason why Transformers are more vulnerable to privacy attacks. We hope our discovery can shed some new light on how to defend against the investigated privacy attacks and help the community build privacy-friendly model architectures. source_intervals.text: Knowledge Unlearning for Mitigating Privacy Risks in Language Models Pretrained Language Models (LMs) memorize a vast amount of knowledge during initial pretraining, including information that may violate the privacy of personal lives and identities. Previous work addressing privacy issues for language models has mostly focused on data preprocessing and differential privacy methods, both requiring re-training the underlying LM. We show that simply performing gradient ascent on target token sequences is effective at forgetting them with little to no degradation of general language modeling performances for larger LMs; it sometimes even substantially improves the underlying LM with just a few iterations. By showing comparisons with a previous data preprocessing method and a decoding method known to mitigate privacy risks for LMs, we show that unlearning can give a stronger empirical privacy guarantee in scenarios where the data vulnerable to extraction attacks are known a priori while being much more efficient and robust. source_intervals.text: Provably Confidential Language Modelling Large language models are shown to memorize privacy information such as social security numbers in training data. Given the sheer scale of the training corpus, it is challenging to screen and filter these privacy data, either manually or automatically. In this paper, we propose Confidentially Redacted Training (CRT), a method to train language generation models while protecting the confidential segments. source_intervals.text: Submix: Practical Private Prediction for Large-Scale Language Models Recent data-extraction attacks have exposed that language models can memorize some training samples verbatim. source_intervals.text: Validating Large Language Models with ReLM Although large language models (LLMs) have been touted for their ability to generate natural-sounding text, there are growing concerns around possible negative effects of LLMs such as data memorization, bias, and inappropriate language. Unfortunately, the complexity and generation capacities of LLMs make validating (and correcting) such concerns difficult. In this work, we introduce ReLM, a system for validating and querying LLMs using standard regular expressions. ReLM formalizes and enables a broad range of language model evaluations, reducing complex evaluation rules to simple regular expression queries. Our results exploring queries surrounding memorization, gender bias, toxicity, and language understanding show that ReLM achieves up to 15x higher system efficiency, 2.5x data efficiency, and increased statistical and prompt-tuning coverage compared to state-of-the-art ad-hoc queries. ReLM offers a competitive and general baseline for the increasingly important problem of LLM validation. sections.title: 研究问题与技术前史
sections.body: 语言模型隐私泄露的研究起源于神经网络对训练数据的记忆特性及其带来的信息重构风险。在早期探索中，研究者试图厘清语言模型记忆行为与数据泄露之间的映射关系。针对LSTM等循环神经网络语言模型的分析表明，困惑度（perplexity）较低的句子更易被模型深度记忆，从而成为隐私攻击的脆弱点。为了在源头阻断这一风险，早期的防御分支之一是直接对训练材料进行干预，通过语义变异（mutating）训练数据来实现模型的“去记忆化”（dememorization），且该机制在评估中能够在不折损模型效用的前提下缓解数据泄露[11]。随着隐私保护理论的引入，差分隐私（DP）成为演进路线上的另一核心分支。在循环语言模型的早期联邦训练中，研究者通过改造联邦平均算法，实现了用户级别的差分隐私保障；该机制的核心发现是，当参与用户规模足够大时，引入隐私噪声的主要代价是计算开销的增加，而非传统认为的模型效用骤降[1]。当研究主体向BERT等预训练语言模型演进时，隐私注入的机制发生了分化。与传统的全局梯度加噪不同，部分研究转向局部差分隐私（Local DP）设定，通过在输入文本或词嵌入（token embeddings）等不同前向阶段施加约束，探索隐私自适应的预训练方法，从而缓解了自然语言理解任务在直接应用隐私约束时的适配问题[21]。与此同时，分布式架构的演进催生了对联邦学习场景下语言模型隐私威胁的重新审视。尽管联邦学习通过仅传输模型更新而非原始数据来构建初步防御，但早期的威胁模型测量表明，这种架构并未彻底消除隐私泄露风险。无论是恶意聚合服务器还是普通参与节点，均可通过深度梯度泄露（Deep Gradients Leakage）攻击或生成对抗网络攻击，从共享参数中逆向推断出用户级别的训练样本。这一阶段的研究不仅明确了推理攻击推断样本与投毒攻击破坏模型完整性的机制差别，也促使后续防护策略从单一的数据端掩码向聚合端的安全汇聚技术演进[49]。

sections.title: 评价对象、威胁模型与测量
sections.body:
语言模型的隐私泄露研究在评价对象、威胁模型与测量方法上经历了系统性演进。

**评价对象的延伸**
早期的评价对象集中于生成式语言模型对训练数据的精确记忆，研究表明模型参数规模越大，记忆现象越严重且脆弱性越高[4]。随着研究深入，评估对象扩展至非生成式任务。文本分类模型同样存在数据提取风险，攻击者可利用目标标签的似然度推断输入中缺失的词元[43]；或通过模型反演，利用预训练生成模型（如GPT-2）构建模板并依据分类器反馈进行扰动，从而重建私有训练文本[52]。此外，文本嵌入（Embeddings）也成为重要的评价对象。研究证实，密集嵌入向量不仅保留了语义，还可通过逆向优化恢复大部分输入词汇，甚至被用于推断疾病部位或作者身份等独立于主任务的敏感属性[5][7]。

**威胁模型的复杂化**
威胁模型从简单的黑盒查询演进为多阶段、动态与对抗性环境下的复杂攻击。在模型提取攻击中，攻击者仅需向API发送随机词序列（乱码数据），即可成功克隆BERT类模型[3]；这种攻击甚至能从单语受害者模型中提取出具备多语言能力的副本[9]。更为严重的是，这种提取过程会继承并暴露原始数据的隐私，使得针对克隆副本的属性推断攻击同样能够窃取受害者训练集信息[38]。

在动态更新场景下，攻击者利用模型更新前后的参数快照实施差分分析，可通过束搜索算法精准提取新增的对话数据[2]；对于智能回复等微调应用，灰盒快照攻击通过对比微调前后的标记概率变化，能够成功提取密码和邮箱等敏感模式[25]。在联邦学习等去中心化架构中，威胁模型被进一步强化：恶意服务器可通过部署篡改的参数字典，单独提取Transformer的标记嵌入与位置嵌入，进而高保真地重建长序列用户文本[28]。此外，数据投毒成为一种新型机制，攻击者仅需篡改不足0.1%的训练数据，便能引导模型将特定目标视为异常，从而使成员推理等隐私推断的成功率跃升一至两个数量级[56]。

**测量机制的校准**
随着攻击机制的精细化，隐私泄露的测量指标也得到了根本性校正。过往研究常采用平均分类准确率来衡量成员推理攻击，但这一对称指标掩盖了真实的安全威胁。现代测量主张在极低假阳性率（如<0.1%）下计算真阳性率，以评估攻击是否能以高置信度识别特定成员[16]。在针对掩码语言模型（MLM）的评估中，传统的单一模型置信度测量往往失效；通过引入参考模型构建基于能量的似然比假设检验，攻击在1%假阳性率下的效力可提升数十倍，AUC指标也获得了显著修正[45]。为了统一复杂场景的测量基准，研究者提出了参数化评估框架（如KART），将隐私泄露风险分解为先验知识、数据匿名化程度、外部语料资源及目标实体等维度，为语言模型隐私审计提供了系统性标准[13]。

sections.title: 基准构建、检测与防护
sections.body: 语言模型隐私防护已演进为在训练、微调及推理阶段组合数据去重、选择性差分隐私与生成扰动的多维机制。早期全局差分隐私（DP）虽提供理论保证，但导致显著的效用下降。为优化隐私与效用的联合空间，[20]引入对抗鉴别器与三元组损失正则化；[44]结合编辑与随机化机制实现机密编辑训练（CRT），在特定任务上维持了与基线相近的困惑度。针对特定实体的隐私泄露，[23]提出选择性差分隐私（S-DP），仅对通过策略函数检测到的敏感词元添加噪声；[57]进一步结合用户与实体采样，提出用户-实体差分隐私（UeDP）以优化模型敏感度上界。在数据层面，[29]发现模型记忆率与训练集中序列重复次数呈超线性相关，数据去重可显著降低记忆攻击的成功率。[55]验证了T5模型的跨度破坏目标比传统的下个词预测更具抗记忆性。在微调与分布式架构下，大模型的参数规模放大了DP噪声。为降低计算与隐私成本，[36]在微调阶段引入Edgeworth会计师，提供非渐进的有限样本隐私边界。[14]通过避免实例化线性层的逐样本梯度，使得在适度语料上直接进行DP-SGD微调的内存开销与非隐私训练相当。在联邦学习场景中，[54]提出部分嵌入更新（PEU）以降低大词表传输中的DP噪声；[30]通过输入加密优化问题（LODA）直接学习模糊化数据特征以防御梯度泄露；[46]则证明在训练时冻结词嵌入可有效防御大批量文本的梯度反演恢复攻击（FILM）。针对免重训的后置防护，机制开始向推理端转移。[33]在解码阶段对输出概率分布应用轻量级扰动，通过后处理特性继承隐私优势。[51]的SubMix协议通过集成模型的子样本聚合松弛群组DP，在预测时限制单用户特有信息的泄露。[40]提出知识遗忘机制，通过对目标序列执行梯度上升，在先验已知易受攻击数据时提供比预处理更强的经验隐私保证。

sections.title: 有效性、鲁棒性和外推边界
sections.body:
语言模型隐私攻防的演进不仅体现在技术手段的更迭，更在于其有效性、鲁棒性及外推边界的显著拓展。在攻击外推边界方面，早期的模型逆向和成员推理通常依赖严苛的先验假设。然而，近期的研究发现迁移学习打破了这一安全错觉：微调模型与预训练基座在权重分布上存在极高相似性，攻击者仅需利用框架或硬件的特定计算签名，即可推断出黑盒模型的基座架构并逆向完整权重[47]。与此同时，数据恢复攻击的鲁棒性也得到增强。传统重构依赖目标样本的真实标签预测，但基于分布判别的提取机制无需真实类别先验，仅通过伪标签预测与分布差异即可实现相似的隐私数据还原率，极大拓宽了预训练模型泄漏威胁的外推边界[48]。

在防御机制的有效性演进上，差分隐私（DP）的实施路径出现了从反向传播向正向传播和参数高效微调的分支转移。传统的DP-SGD在反向传播阶段对梯度进行裁剪与加噪，不仅引入梯度偏差，还会在大模型上引发严重的内存开销。相比之下，差分隐私正向传播机制通过在正向阶段直接对潜层表示进行裁剪加噪，并结合微批次子采样实现隐私放大，从而在保持梯度无偏的同时大幅缓解了性能降级[10]。此外，模型规模与隐私效用之间展现出反直觉的关联外推性：在参数高效微调框架下，随着语言模型参数量级的提升，其在注入相同隐私预算噪声时的鲁棒性反而更强，能够在维持严格隐私约束下逼近非隐私模型的效用表现[12]。

针对分布式与表示层的隐私保护，机制有效性从单一表示扰动向混合理论约束演进。在联邦学习场景中，早期的实例编码机制主要通过对预训练模型的输入表示应用单次密钥加密或混合以抵御梯度窃听[8]。然而，由于缺乏理论隐私下界，单纯的实例编码极易受重构攻击破解。为此，后继方法将差分隐私机制与实例编码深度融合，通过在特征提取层引入拉普拉斯或高斯噪声，建立了抵抗重构攻击的可证明隐私边界[34]。此外，在对话聊天机器人外推至用户级特征保护时，隐藏状态极易过度拟合发音者的私人画像。通过在防御目标中引入互信息损失与KL散度惩罚，可直接将攻击者对人物属性的后验预测分布扁平化，在阻断画像推断攻击的同时，有效保留了语言模型的生成鲁棒性[61]。

sections.title: 实验证据与方法比较
sections.body:
语言模型隐私泄露的实验评估经历了从单一场景向标准化框架与细粒度指标的演进。早期研究因攻击假设不一难以横向比较，研究者提出KART（知识、匿名化、资源与目标）参数化框架以统一成员推理等泄露场景的定义标准[6]。在评价指标层面，除了传统的生成重叠率，研究者通过对比私有模型与公共模型生成的独有序列数量，量化了模型生成训练集中独有句子片段的泄露风险[19]；同时采用“暴露度”（Exposure）指标评估随机金丝雀样本提取对攻击者猜测熵的降低程度[41]。面对大型语言模型庞大的生成解空间，通过正则表达式将复杂的记忆验证规则转化为有限状态自动机查询，不仅规避了临时采样的偏差，还显著提升了评估的系统效率与统计覆盖率[58]。

在比较机制与对照条件方面，模型架构与规模表现出显著的隐私脆弱性差异。研究表明，由于注意力模块及偏置参数的设计特征，Transformer架构整体比传统卷积神经网络更容易受到多种隐私推理攻击[39]。在语言模型内部，掩码语言模型的经验隐私泄露水平通常低于自回归模型[15]。关于模型规模的实验结果呈现出多维度的冲突现象：一方面，小型模型的经验泄露总体低于大型模型[15]，且模型复杂度与预训练数据量的增加会正向推高信息泄露风险[60]；另一方面，动态跟踪训练过程发现，大模型不仅能以更少优化步数完成精确记忆（特别是优先记忆作为数据标识符的名词与数字），甚至在不过拟合的情况下保留更多早期训练记忆，导致其遗忘率反而低于小规模基线[42]。此外，实验证实模型虽然能够深度记忆邮箱地址等私有片段，但缺乏将上下文特征与特定实体强关联的能力，导致零样本条件下的直接提取成功率极低[26]。

针对分布式部署与多模态融合条件的评估揭示了不同环境下的真实威胁边界。在联邦学习框架中，中心化学习下普遍存在的非预期记忆倾向，会因联邦架构自带的按用户聚类机制及大批次聚合而得到大幅缓解[24]。然而，理论上的差分隐私界限在联邦环境中可能过于保守，基于恶意客户端构造特定金丝雀样本并观测异常模型更新的经验测量表明，实际的隐私暴露风险（经验$\epsilon$值）比理论上限低两至七倍[27]。在多模态融合场景中，即便攻击者只能通过合成音频进行端到端语音识别的黑盒查询，利用基线与金丝雀样本的词错率差异，依然能检测出融合语言模型对仅出现一次的文本序列的无意记忆，且该记忆水平随模型容量增加而放大[31]。

防护机制的引入进一步凸显了隐私与效用的权衡冲突。在多语言情感分析等任务中，差分隐私的强噪声注入会严重损害模型的下游效用[60]；但在层次化文本分类等特定任务中，针对长文本优化的Transformer模型即便在较大的差分隐私参数下，也能在完全防御白盒成员推理攻击的同时维持合理的预测性能[18]。相比于后置扰动，在预处理阶段执行严格的自动去标识化，不仅不会阻碍临床语言模型的领域适应，反而在部分下游任务中实现了效用的微幅提升，为规避记忆风险提供了低成本的对照验证方案[35]。

sections.title: 局限、效率与开放问题
sections.body:
语言模型隐私保护的演进不仅受制于工程层面的技术瓶颈，更面临理论假设与自然语言特性的根本失配。传统数据清理与差分隐私（DP）机制高度依赖数据的结构化特征与逻辑独立性假设，这与自然语言高度语境化且缺乏明确个体或相邻界定的本质产生了直接冲突[32][59]。在基础模型层面，这种理论局限性被进一步放大：由于处理异构用户数据需要满足极高的所罗门诺夫-柯尔莫哥洛夫复杂度，模型必须通过深度记忆来实现任务泛化，这使得在超高维参数空间下追求高准确率与保障严格隐私安全，在数学基础上存在难以调和的内在不兼容性[50]。

当前主流的模型防护机制在特定边界条件下表现出明显的失效特征。在词级别差分隐私中，距离度量机制容易在长文本序列中隐性吸收隐私损失，导致在未能有效掩盖原作者风格特征的情况下过早消耗了理论隐私预算[53]。同时，针对文本表示层的实例编码混合机制同样缺乏严密的安全性下界，攻击者无需付出高昂的计算代价，即可通过模型逆向攻击以高成功率重建出原始敏感文本向量[22]。此外，即便防御方将嵌入层置于黑盒部署环境中以隐藏内部状态，成员推断攻击依然能绕过高成本的影子模型训练，将底层语义泄露风险直接穿透至下游的文本分类与自然语言生成任务中[17]。

在部署成本与训练效率维度，差分隐私的引入从根本上打破了语言模型的常规缩放定律。在非隐私环境下普遍适用的“模型参数越大性能越好”经验法则在DP-SGD优化中彻底失效，不同复杂度任务的隐私防护呈现出高度的架构与策略依赖：例如，受限于梯度裁剪与噪声注入，参数量更小的蒸馏模型虽能通过降低显存占用换取更大的训练批次，但在面对多类别序列标注等复杂任务时，其性能反而出现严重退化[62]。更为严峻的未解决问题在于隐私效用与算法公平性之间的冲突，差分隐私的梯度更新会对少数群体的特征表示产生不成比例的损害，在稳健深度学习体系中呈现出隐私预算与公平性指标的对数级负相关；理论推导证明，当模型被同时强制要求满足绝对差分隐私与严格组等风险公平时，其预测结果将完全退化为与输入数据无关的平凡输出[37]。
